nameStory: Siberian bugloss gets its name from the region where it was first discovered growing wild - not actually Siberia, but the Caucasus mountains near the Black Sea. The 'bugloss' part comes from an old Greek word meaning 'ox tongue,' referring to the rough, tongue-like texture of the leaves that you can feel when you run your fingers across them.
description: Siberian bugloss is a low-growing perennial that forms attractive clumps of large, heart-shaped leaves in shady garden spots. It reaches about 12-18 inches tall and spreads slowly to create excellent groundcover. In spring, it sends up delicate sprays of tiny blue flowers that look remarkably like forget-me-nots, blooming for 8-10 weeks before the heart-shaped leaves take center stage for the rest of the growing season.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large heart-shaped leaves about 6 inches across with a distinctly rough, sandpaper-like texture when touched. Many garden varieties have striking white or cream markings that make them look almost painted.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright blue flowers in loose, airy clusters that look exactly like forget-me-nots but appear on much taller, more delicate stems above the foliage in mid-spring.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, slowly spreading clumps that stay low to the ground, with leaves emerging directly from the base on slender stems rather than from a central woody trunk.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Leaf stems are thin and somewhat fragile, while flower stems are even more delicate and branching, creating an almost cloud-like effect above the foliage.

habitat: In New England, Siberian bugloss is found almost exclusively in cultivated gardens and landscaped areas, especially in shady spots under trees or along building foundations. It thrives in moist, well-drained soil and has occasionally escaped cultivation to naturalize in similar shady, protected areas near human habitation.

seasonality.spring: The star of the show - sends up delicate sprays of tiny blue flowers in mid-spring that bloom for 8-10 weeks, while fresh heart-shaped leaves emerge from the ground.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the large, textured heart-shaped leaves remain prominent and attractive, often showing cream or white variegation in cultivated varieties.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may begin to yellow and die back, and this is the best time to divide established clumps if you want to propagate them.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, leaving no visible trace until spring emergence.

funFact: This plant may be a living window into ancient history - genetic evidence suggests that Siberian bugloss reflects what forests around the Black Sea looked like millions of years ago, making your garden a tiny time capsule of prehistoric plant life!
confusionNotes: The flowers look nearly identical to true forget-me-nots, but the massive heart-shaped leaves are the giveaway - forget-me-nots have small, narrow leaves. Remember: big heart leaves = Siberian bugloss, tiny leaves = forget-me-not.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, Siberian bugloss isn't actually from Siberia but from the Caucasus region. It's also called 'great forget-me-not' because of its larger size compared to true forget-me-nots, though they're closely related in the borage family.
compareHints: Siberian bugloss is the only Brunnera species commonly grown in New England gardens. Compared to other borage family members like true forget-me-nots, it's distinguished by its much larger size and prominent heart-shaped basal leaves. Unlike the weedy forget-me-nots that pop up everywhere, Siberian bugloss stays put in neat, well-behaved clumps.
